The last time I was physically here at Kauffman Stadium for a baseball game was on September 4, where I witnessed Daniel Lynch IV immediately give up five runs in two innings and functionally take the Royals out of the contest before it began. I got worked up enough about it that I wrote about it that weekend, where I said that the Lynch starter experiment was going exactly how everyone knew it would because of Lynch’s inability to get right-handed batters out with his awful changeup. I linked multiple videos of Lynch hanging changes on a line to those righties.
You can therefore imagine my displeasure at walking into the clubhouse this afternoon, checking my phone to see who was officially starting, and seeing Lynch’s name pop up. I feared a Groundhog’s Day situation.
Unfortunately for me and the meager collection of Royals die-hards watching in person, that’s what happened. The White Sox crushed Royals pitching to the tune of 14 runs, and no amount of late game heroics could lessen the gap. Final score: 14-11, White Sox.
It began early. Witness this rocket line drive off a changeup in the first inning! It was from right-handed batter Chase Meidroth.
Oh, and this laser of an opposite-field home run from right-handed Brenton Doyle. It came off, you guessed it, a changeup.
And this—hark! Another Meidroth homer off another changeup!
After three innings, the White Sox had thwomped their way to a 6-0 lead, which was cut to a whole 6-1 lead by a solo Nick Loftin home run in the bottom of the sixth.
But Lynch was still pitching, and so you could probably bet that five-run lead might balloon further. Sure enough, it did. In the fourth inning, Lynch managed to get two outs but then ran into a row of right-handed batters and, well. You know what happened. Miguel Vargas single, Tommy Pham walk, Randal Grichuk home run. 9-1, White Sox.
At this point, I packed up my belongings and left to listen to the game on the drive and follow from home. Getting credentials is an honor, but what is also great is that, since I’m not a beat writer, I can bail when it’s clear that postgame pressers are not going to yield any particularly interesting pieces of information. Both teams packed it in after the seventh inning; the White Sox removed Miguel Vargas, Tommy Pham, and Braden Montgomery, while the Royals removed Bobby Witt Jr. and Salvador Perez.
Kansas City’s offense, however, did not go quietly into the night. The Royals struck in three consecutive innings against Chicago starter Anthony Kay, with Witt accruing three hits. They managed a trio of runs against Trevor Richards in the eighth, with a pair of extra base hits by the Italian Stallions Jac Caglianone and Vinnie Pasquantino providing the power. And then, in the ninth inning, Tyler Tolbert singled, and Caglianone singled, and Maikel Garcia worked his third walk of the game. Pasquantino then crushed a grand slam to right-center field. It was glorious.
But any hope the Royals had of a great comeback was stymied by, you guessed it, the bullpen. In his Royals debut and his 2026 debut, Tony Gonsolin—who has only pitched 36 MLB innings the last two seasons due to injury—pitched two clean innings and exploded in the seventh, giving up a double to Grichuk and a homer to Munetaka Murakami. Then, he loaded the bases and walked home another run, which prompted Matt Quatraro to remove him in favor of Nolan Hoffman. Hoffman immediately gave up a single to Andrew Benintendi to push the score to 14-4.
As a result, even though the Royals scored 11 runs, they didn’t score a single run down by less than six. Since August 30, the Royals have won two (2) games where they have scored fewer than five runs. That’s because they’ve given up, on average, 5.5 games during that 20-game span.
This is the Royals’ fifth consecutive loss, their eighth loss in their last nine games, and their 15th in their last 20. Remember when the Royals won 13 of 15? They were 13 games under .500 after that first win.
Tonight, the Royals officially wipe all those gains away, and are now 13 games under again. Winning 70 games seems like a longshot. Eat Arby’s.

item.content:encoded:
When Aaron Judge is healthy, he’s the most dangerous hitter in baseball. Sometimes I get alarmed at how uncontroversial a statement that is; ours is a sport that so frequently humiliates those who make such sweeping, unequivocal judgments as those.
But the empirical evidence is what it is. Judge has played 150 or more games in a season four times in his career. In those four seasons, he’s led all position players in WAR four times and led the league in wRC+ three times. He’s been named AL MVP three times and finished second once, ahead of some real doozies: Cal Raleigh’s 60-homer year, Bobby Witt Jr.’s 10.5-WAR campaign in 2024, Shohei Ohtani’s best pitching season — in fact, a healthy Judge is the only thing that’s ever trumped a healthy Ohtani in an MVP race.
So again, it’s not uncontroversial to say that when Judge is healthy he’s the best hitter in the world. He has not, however, always been healthy. Least of all this season, when he missed three months with a broken rib. And now, the single-season AL home run king is back on the IL with a calf strain. The timing could not be worse.
Judge last played on Wednesday, leaving open the option to activate him on Sunday for the final game of the regular season. That seems like a theoretical concern at the moment rather than a practical one. Our Matt Martell was at Yankee manager Aaron Boone’s pregame media availability on Tuesday morning, where Boone illustrated the inadequacy of a return-to-play timeline at this point in the season.
“We’re planning on [Judge] not being a part of [the Wild Card Series],” Boone said. “You hear all the time with injuries, we give ranges: two to four weeks, four to six. They’re ranges for a reason. We’re at a point in the year where, obviously, we’d push it a little bit if that was in play, but that’s a week away. I’m not expecting it, but I’m not ruling it out either.”
That’s the problem. A range of two weeks in recovery time isn’t a big deal in a six-month season, but even one week is twice as long as the Yankees’ entire first playoff round. And muscle injuries can be finicky to begin with — you go to bed one night feeling fine and wake up the next morning with weakness or stiffness.
For what it’s worth, the Yankees are technically still alive in the AL East race as of this writing, but you can forgive Boone for speaking as if the division is already lost.
Either way, in order to speed things along, Judge received a platelet-poor plasma (PPP) injection on Monday, not to be confused with a platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection.
Now, apparently having read The Magic School Bus Inside the Human Body as a child is not a sufficient qualification to perform surgery on live patients. At least, that’s what the police told me. But anyone who’s read that book can tell you the makeup of human blood: Red blood cells, which carry oxygen; white blood cells, which fight infection; platelets, which stop bleeding and heal wounds; and plasma, which is the broth all the other stuff floats around in.
PRP injections are a pretty common treatment for sports injuries, but taking the healing bits out of plasma seems kind of counterintuitive. Sort of like a vodka-poor screwdriver. But evidently PPP contains high levels of fibrinogen, which is itself a healing agent. Ms. Frizzle didn’t cover fibrinogen, but sure, I’ll buy it.
Unless the PPP works an actual miracle, though, it looks like the Yankees are going to have to navigate at least the first round of the playoffs without their best player.
And even if Judge does return — either in the Wild Card round or later, if the Yankees advance — I’d caution against assuming that we’d be seeing the best of him right off the proverbial bat. For starters, 99% of star athletes in history are going to try to force their way into the lineup for the playoffs regardless of whether they’re actually healthy.
To say nothing of the fact that Judge can be streaky. This is the nature of Judge’s unusual skill set; there are 1,073 hitters in major league history with at least 5,000 career plate appearances. Judge is the only one of those who’s produced one of the three true outcomes (home run, strikeout, walk) in more than half of his career plate appearances. (I’d like to express my immense gratitude to Adam Dunn, who has a career TTO% of 49.9, for making this fun fact possible.)
Living on the extremes, as he does, Judge will have weeks where he homers every night, and others where he goes 1-for-20 with 12 strikeouts. But you live with it because, over a long enough timeline, it works out heavily in his favor. Among hitters with at least 5,000 career plate appearances, Judge has the third-highest career wRC+, trailing only Babe Ruth and Ted Williams. If you wanted to go further than “best hitter now” and anoint Judge the best hitter ever, leaning heavily on the argument that quality of competition increases over time, you’d have a credible case.
But that’s not what the Yankees got out of Judge this year. In 66 regular-season games, he’s hit .241/.360/.511, with his highest strikeout rate (29.8%) since 2019 and lowest wRC+ (141) since 2020. In seven games since he returned from his rib injury, Judge was just 4-for-23 with one home run, one walk, and 13 strikeouts.
I’ve done enough of these injury reaction posts to figure out that they’re not really about the guy who got hurt, but about the teammates he’s leaving behind.
And I don’t want to underrate the value of Judge — even the version of Judge that has a 141 wRC+, rather than a 200 wRC+ — but the Yankees have done OK without him.
In the weakest American League field in decades, the Yankees are one of only two teams with a winning percentage of .550 or better. Entering their doubleheader with the Rays on Tuesday, the Yankees are still first in the AL in home runs (216) and second in runs scored per game (4.60). Even without Judge (or Giancarlo Stanton, for that matter), their lineup has plenty of beef.

Ben Rice in particular has been absolutely terrific this season. He’s fourth among qualified AL hitters in wRC+ and third in both home runs and runs scored. The Astros have AL MVP frontrunner Yordan Alvarez in their lineup; apart from him, is there any hitter in the AL bracket who’s been Rice’s equal this year? Maybe Junior Caminero? Willson Contreras, if you value OBP over raw power? Even if you’re being charitable, it’s a short list.
Now, past Rice, things get interesting, because if you want to talk about the Yankees’ offensive depth, you have to be able to hold multiple ideas in your head at once.
As of Tuesday morning, the Yankees have 11 hitters with double-digit home runs this season, which is tied for the most in the league. That’s just counting players who have hit 10 or more home runs in pinstripes, and the Yankees brought in substantial reinforcements midseason. Luis García Jr. has just seven homers for the Yankees but 30 overall. Heliot Ramos has four home runs in 32 games and 13 overall, with 20-plus in each of his previous two seasons. George Lombard Jr. has just five home runs in 37 major league games, but he hit 12 dingers in 78 minor league games before he got called up.
Count all this up and the Yankees have more hitters with at least decent pop than they can fit on the roster at once.
At the same time, Rice is the only Yankee with 20 home runs in pinstripes this year. So while this lineup is short on automatic outs, if Judge is out, there’s a massive drop-off after Rice.
If you take Judge out of the picture, Cody Bellinger is second on the Yankees in wRC+, at 119. The Rays don’t have anyone with 100 or more plate appearances and a better wRC+ than Rice this season, but they have four hitters (Caminero, Yandy Díaz, Jonathan Aranda, and Victor Mesa Jr.) with 100 or more plate appearances and a better wRC+ than Bellinger. So do the Rangers (Justin Foscue, Josh Jung, Joc Pederson, Wyatt Langford). The Astros have Alvarez, plus Isaac Paredes and Jeremy Peña. The White Sox have Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami, and Tristan Peters.
As good as Rice has been, the Yankees’ lineup looks concerningly pedestrian without Judge. If you aren’t already a FanGraphs Member, please consider becoming one; it’s the only way to get trenchant original analysis like this.
The good news is that Judge’s calf injury runs counter to the rest of the team’s injury luck. Carlos Rodón, who missed almost three months with an elbow injury earlier this year, dominated the Rays in eight scoreless innings in Game 1 of a doubleheader on Tuesday. The same day, the Yankees activated Chisholm, who’d spent two weeks on the IL with a sprained thumb. Clarke Schmidt just returned from Tommy John surgery last week, and while he suffered biceps cramping in the bullpen on Sunday, it appears to be a minor setback. Trent Grisham remains a question mark for the start of the playoffs as he recovers from a hamstring injury, but his prognosis also looks good.
Judge is as important to the Yankees as any two or three other players put together, but with a healthy and deep rotation and Rice leading the way offensively, they’re not in bad shape. The remainder of this roster could easily survive and advance through a weaker AL bracket, setting the stage for a dramatically timed Judge return in mid-October. Like Kirk Gibson, only bigger.
Michael is a writer at FanGraphs. Previously, he was a staff writer at The Ringer and D1Baseball, and his work has appeared at Grantland, Baseball Prospectus, The Atlantic, ESPN.com, and various ill-remembered Phillies blogs. Follow him on Twitter, if you must, @MichaelBaumann.

item.content:encoded:
The future couldn’t have looked better for the Kansas City Royals in 2024. They had one of baseball’s brightest young stars in Bobby Witt Jr. and reached the postseason for the first time in nine years.
Two years later, the Royals still have Witt and the 26-year-old three-time All-Star shortstop remains one of baseball’s top young players. However, the Royals’ postseason run, which included upsetting the Baltimore Orioles in an American League Wild Card Series, seems like eons ago.
The Royals are 67-89 going into their final six games and are likely to finish last in the AL Central. That is quite a drop from their 86-76 record two years ago and even their 82-80 mark of last season.
Witt isn’t going anywhere. He is signed through 2030 and there are player and team options from 2031-37 in Witt’s seven-year, $148.78-million contract.
Bobby Witt Jr. and the Royals aren't heading in the right direction
Witt’s career continues to ascend as his 6.5 bWAR this season is third in the AL behind New York Yankees right-hander Cam Schlittler (7.0) and Detroit Tigers rookie infielder Kevin McGonigle (6.7). Witt is hitting .279/.359/.440 with 18 home runs and 43 stolen bases in 137 games.
Yet the Royals are descending as they have the fifth-worst record in the major leagues. It’s hard not to think that the franchise is beginning to waste a golden opportunity while having Witt under contract.
| Team | Win % |
|---|---|
| Royals | .429 |
| Giants | .414 |
| Athletics | .391 |
| Angels | .385 |
| Rockies | .365 |
Witt is obviously disappointed with the way this season has played out. However, he is not the type of person who is going to publicly going to criticize the organization or tell president of baseball operations J.J. Piccolo how to do his job.
“I think we need some pieces, which you can tell from looking at our record,” Witt told FanSided. “But I know for me personally and most of the guys that the season has been disappointing in the sense that it hasn’t come close to turning out like we wanted it to just because we didn't perform the way we wanted to. We felt like we had the team to go where we wanted to go in spring training and coming into the season.”
The last time the Royals were over .500 was on April Fools Day when they beat the visiting Minnesota Twins 13-9 at Kauffman Stadium to improve to 3-2. An eight-game losing streak from April 12-20 dropped the Royals to 7-16 and they’ve never recovered despite having a nine-game winning streak in August.
“We just got away from playing good baseball this year,” Witt said. “We just need to get back to playing our game, not overthinking things and just doing the little things that can make us a good team.
“I think it's just kind of make sure we're just focused each and every day, focus on our work, and that the emphasis has to be on doing whatever we can to win each night’s game.”
The Royals have not been good on either side of the ball. They are 24th in MLB in runs scored with 4.21 per game and 25th in runs allowed with a 4.86 average.
Why Bobby Witt Jr. shoulders the blame for Royals tough season
Though Witt ranks among the AL leaders in bWAR, he is not happy about his season and takes his share of the responsibility for the lost season.
“It’s one of those things where you learn a lot about who you are individually and how you can become better,” Witt said. “I feel like that's something to take away from this year. Learn how to kind of be more mentally sound throughout the entire year going through the bumps and bruises throughout a long season and trying to get better every day.”
The Royals, though, do not plan to rebuild this upcoming winter. Piccolo signaled that the Royals plan to contend next season at this year’s trade deadline when he surprisingly rebuffed offers for veteran right-hander Michael Wacha, who has one year remaining on his contract.
Witt is one of four players in the lineup who is 26 or younger, giving the Royals potentially the foundation of a good team. Catcher Carter Jensen’s 25 home runs are a franchise single season record for a rookie. Right fielder Jac Caglianone has 23 homers, 71 RBIs and a team-leading .821 OPS. Though his season has been ruined by a torn hamstring, third baseman Maikel Garcia was an All-Star last year.
“All you ever want is to play in the postseason and it was so much fun two years ago,” Witt said. “To kind of take a step back from that, you get frustrated. You also got to learn from it, build from it and just know that there's a lot of work to do to get back to that position.”

On Sunday, as MLB’s regular season reached its one-week warning, the two most spectacular players of 2026 strutted their stuff. In Cincinnati, Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong singled, doubled, and hit his 45th home run in a 9-1 trouncing of the Reds. (He also stole his 38th base, putting him on the precipice of joining the 40-40 club.) Hours later, at Camden Yards, Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski held the Orioles to one hit and lowered his ERA to 1.86 as the Brewers blanked Baltimore 3-0 for their major-league-leading (and franchise-record) 98th win.
A season’s most sensational player isn’t always its most valuable player—see Cal Raleigh last year—but PCA and the Miz check both boxes. They lead the majors in FanGraphs WAR for hitters and pitchers, respectively, and will win the MVP and Cy Young awards in the National League (which has established itself as the stronger circuit by owning the American League 375–323 in interleague play). PCA and the Miz; the Miz and PCA: Already All-Stars in 2025, they’ve made large leaps this year. The Cub has bolstered his bat speed and drawn more walks; the Brewer has upped his pitch speed and issued fewer walks. Born nine days apart in the spring of 2002, the two 24-year-old terrors of the NL Central have set the standards for hitting and pitching excellence and, in the process, made themselves the player stories of the season. In an MLB campaign whose compressed standings have caused fans to wonder which teams, if any, are actually good (especially in the AL, where the .500 Rangers lead the AL West), the left-handed hitter and right-handed hurler—whose clubs may meet in October—have left little doubt about their own extreme skills.
There’s also little doubt about how those skills stack up against each other—or, at least, what those skills are worth when they’re applied on the field. The “WAR leader” label lumps PCA and Misiorowski together as peerless players. If we had to choose between them, though, the answer would be easy: The Miz wins most of their head-to-head battles, but PCA wins the WAR. Crow-Armstrong, who’s hit .280/.371/.578 with superlative defense in center, has been much more valuable than Misiorowski, who’s held hitters to a .159/.225/.250 line and who’s struck out 247 batters (including PCA six times) while walking only 42 (including PCA twice). That’s no surprise: It’s now the norm for baseball’s best hitter to be a good deal better, WAR-wise, than baseball’s best pitcher. Which, in turn, tells us a lot about how hitter and pitcher usage—and entertainment value—have evolved.
Take Sunday’s action. PCA played the whole game in center, even though the Cubs had built a comfortable lead by the halfway point. The Miz, meanwhile, exited after three innings and 44 pitches, with the Brew Crew clinging to a 1-0 lead. With home field advantage throughout October up for grabs, Milwaukee still had something to play for. But the Brewers elected to take it easy on their flamethrower, who has already exceeded his 2025 workload (including the playoffs) by 28 innings. As a result, Misiorowski amassed just 62 percent of the WAR PCA did on Sunday—and, on the whole, he’s managed only 63 percent of the WAR PCA has produced this season (6.5 vs. 10.4).
It wasn’t always the case that baseball’s best hitter would leave baseball’s best pitcher in his dust on the combined WAR leaderboard. The chart below compares the values of FanGraphs’ hitting and pitching WAR leaders for each season dating back to the beginning of the DH era in 1973. To smooth out year-to-year variation, each bar represents a five-year rolling average of the annual hitter-minus-pitcher WAR gaps from the listed season plus the four preceding seasons. Thus, the value for 1973 is really the average of the figures from 1969 to 1973, and the value for 2026 is really the average of the figures from 2022 to 2026.
At the dawn of the DH era, when the iron men of the mound were still routinely topping 300 innings, the best pitchers were worth more than the best hitters. Pitchers also reigned supreme around the turn of the century, when the likes of Roger Clemens, Kevin Brown, and Randy Johnson were still topping 250 dominant innings, and Pedro Martínez posted the best pitching season ever by fWAR in 1999 (in a then-paltry 213 1/3 innings, which would lead both leagues in 2026). All in all, from the beginning of the DH era through the end of the 20th century, the leading hitter in any given year was worth only about half a WAR more than the leading pitcher, on average. From 1970 through 2000, the best hitter out-WARed the best pitcher 18 times, while a pitcher took the top spot 13 times. The battle for the title of baseball’s best player was typically close to a toss-up between the most overpowering pitcher and the biggest bat.
Over the past quarter century, though, the hitters have won in a walk. Beginning with 2001, when Barry Bonds morphed into his BALCO-boosted final form, the leading hitter has been about two wins better, on average, than the leading pitcher, enough to declare a conclusive victor despite the metric’s margin of error. During that span, best hitters have led best pitchers 25 seasons to one, with only Corbin Burnes’s slim edge over Trea Turner in 2021 preventing a clean sweep. And the gap is growing: Over the past five years, the leading hitter has been a full four wins better, on average, than the leading pitcher. In other words, baseball’s best pitchers aren’t worth what they used to be—but its best batters are.
This isn’t just a function of the no. 1 hitter lapping the no. 1 pitcher; although the average leads are less pronounced, the same trend appears when we expand the pool to each year’s top five hitters and top five pitchers.
The wide disparity in recent seasons stems in part from an unusually strong run by baseball’s best hitters. The average of 10.4 WAR generated by the hitting WAR leaders in the past five years (Aaron Judge three times, and Ronald Acuña Jr. and PCA once each) is the highest total of any five-season stretch since Bonds, Alex Rodriguez, and Albert Pujols in the early-to-mid 2000s—and, before that, Mickey Mantle, Willie Mays, and Ernie Banks in the late 1950s and Babe Ruth, Jimmie Foxx, and Lou Gehrig in the early 1930s. But it’s also a product of the lowest-ever five-year average WAR tally for pitching pacers (6.4), with the exception of the pandemic-suppressed 2019 to 2023 period and a late-’50s stretch of historically lackluster leading arms.
The culprit isn’t much of a mystery: It’s the playing-time totals. Modern pitchers are working smarter, not harder. (Or, if we want to be charitable, similarly hard, but in shorter bursts.) Collectively, pitchers throw roughly the same number of innings as ever, and accrue just as much WAR. (FanGraphs allots 1,000 WAR leaguewide per season, with 57 percent going to hitters and 43 percent apportioned to pitchers.) But those innings and WAR are distributed across many more arms than they used to be, as innings eating nears extinction and the starting-pitcher protagonist of the past fades from view. This season will either match last year’s all-time full-season low of three 200-plus-inning pitchers, or further reduce the record, depending on whether Michael Wacha (who’s sitting at 194 1/3 frames) joins Sandy Alcantara and Cristopher Sánchez in the 200-inning club in his final start.
Modern major leaguers’ workload diminution is much more apparent for pitchers than hitters. The chart below shows the number of hitters and pitchers who qualified for the batting title and ERA title, respectively, in each season of MLB’s 30-team era (since 1998, excluding 2020). The height of the bars (blue for hitters, orange for pitchers) indicates the number of qualifying players; the numbers above each bar (which could still increase slightly for 2026) denote the average number of plate appearances or innings within each year’s qualifying cohort.
Matt Olson aside, hitters aren’t totally immune to load management. Relative to the late 1990s, the number of qualifying hitters per season has sunk by about 15 percent, and the average number of plate appearances among qualifying hitters has been trimmed by a couple percent. But that’s nothing compared to the cratering of pitcher playing time. The number of qualifying pitchers per season has plummeted by nearly 50 percent, and the average number of innings among the remaining qualifiers has dropped by upwards of 10 percent.
Hence the ho-hum WAR totals mustered of late by baseball’s best pitchers, in an era of familiarity-effect avoidance, rampant pitcher injuries and, relatedly, an increased emphasis on max-effort throwing. As dazzling as today’s top arms are on an inning-per-inning basis—especially fastball-slider monsters like Mason Miller, whose outings are mostly contained to one frame—their GIFable filth comes at a cost. They can’t have both blistering stuff and exceptional staying power.
There’s no perfect substitute for the bulk starters used to supply. In 2019, for instance, Astros starter Gerrit Cole broke J.R. Richard’s single-season franchise record for strikeouts, 40 years after Richard’s nasty 1979 campaign. That accomplishment led to a sentimental meeting on the mound between past and present Astros aces, less than two years before Richard’s death. But although Cole surpassed Richard’s strikeout total, he couldn’t match his complete contribution: Richard threw 80 more innings, and recorded 8.9 WAR to Cole’s 7.5. Even Cole’s 212 1/3 innings in 2019 would be a standout total today; beyond Burnes in 2021, no pitcher since Cole has broken the 7-WAR wall.
On a long enough timescale, almost everything in sports circles back around. Someday, new rules might restore the starter’s lost luster, or overdue expansion might lower the major league replacement level and make the most competent pitchers look like WARlords again. League-leading hitters of the 2020s may be mogging their pitching counterparts when we focus on the DH era, but if we go back to the beginning of the National League, when hurlers who threw 400, 500, or 600 innings ruled the roost, we spot two subsequent stretches when the best bats had it even better than they do now: that late-’50s, offense-friendly low ebb for aces, and the 1920s and early ’30s, when Babe Ruth reinvented offense and broke baseball’s value scale. Once upon a time (or two), this batter-pitcher imbalance wasn’t so strange.
For now, though, we seem to be stuck in a phase where the cream of the crop of pitchers pales in comparison to elite everyday dudes. The sinking ceiling of starting-pitcher value may have implications for how pitchers are paid and staffs are assembled (not to mention how prospects are hyped). Free-agent pitchers make as much money per win as free-agent hitters, but if teams start expecting fewer wins from star pitchers than they do from star hitters, even the scarcity of healthy ligaments might not keep pitcher contracts from shrinking (and dragging down overall player pay). From the fan perspective, though, the more relevant byproduct of this modern mismatch in the value of leading hitters and pitchers is a shift in how we experience and describe standout seasons.
Because hitter playing-time totals today are comparable to what they were a century ago, we can still celebrate league-leading hitters via counting stats alone. PCA, for example, has played in every Cubs game this season, and started all but one. (As of today, he’s the majors’ sole 700-plate-appearance man.) We can convey his greatness just by marveling at how many homers he’s hit and bases he’s swiped; “the first 40-40 center fielder” would sound spiffy. If we want to dig deeper, we could note that only Triple Crown contender Yordan Alvarez stands in the way of PCA becoming the first player ever to lead the majors in both batting and fielding value in a single season, which would be a two-way feat almost as mind-blowing as Shohei Ohtani’s pitching/hitting heroics. And if we want to cite WAR, well, that’s easy: With six Cubs games to go, PCA’s season already ranks among the 50 best batting years in big league history, and above every season in the past half century save for four by Bonds, two by Judge, and one by Bobby Witt Jr.
In 2026, pitchers tend not to throw enough pitches or innings to reach famous milestones in single games, single seasons, or careers, so the case for Miz amazement can’t be made by hailing his membership in exclusive, storied clubs. With one regular-season start remaining, the Miz hasn’t quite cracked the top 350 seasons by pitching WAR. (No pitcher has posted a double-digit-WAR season since the Big Unit in 2001.) The 300-strikeout club has been closed to new recruits since Cole and his teammate Justin Verlander went in together in 2019. As for old-school wins, he’s tied for second in the Senior Circuit with 15, not that anyone pays much attention to that column on the player page.
To appreciate the Miz, we must resort to rate stats and modest minimums. Among pitchers with at least 160 innings in a season, Misiorowski ranks 13th in park- and league-adjusted ERA, 12th in park- and league-adjusted FIP, third in WHIP and strikeout-minus-walk rate, and second in strikeout rate. He has the lowest opponent batting average and rate of hits allowed per nine innings, too, which would be more eye-popping if people still cared about batting average or if the league were hitting more than .244. Ultimately, the summation rests on the smallest of samples: a single pitch. At peak pitch speed, he’s the hardest-throwing starter on record (and in all likelihood, ever), and damn near the hardest-throwing pitcher, period.
In a sense, the Miz is just as impactful as PCA—he just hasn’t had as many chances to make an impact. PCA has paired his 702 trips to the plate (offensive chances, essentially) with 380 chances in center, for a grand total of 1,082 opportunities to determine the outcome of a plate appearance. Misiorowski has faced 646 batters, or 60 percent of PCA’s combined plate appearances plus defensive chances. If we look at things that way—i.e., by doing dubious addition—then the Miz has done well to accumulate 63 percent of PCA’s WAR.
Plus, in defense of Misiorowski and the constellation of starters who trail him by 1 WAR or less—AL Cy Young lock Cam Schlittler, Cristopher Sánchez, Chris Sale, Jesús Luzardo, and Dylan Cease—the tale of the 2026 WAR leader is as much about Crow-Armstrong vs. the field as it is pitchers vs. hitters. Only Ohtani and Witt sit between PCA and Misiorowski on FanGraphs’ WAR leaderboard, and both only barely lead the Miz. WAR is always subject to retroactive updates, but if none of the players clustered between 6.4 and 6.7 WAR—Ohtani, Misiorowski, Witt, and Alvarez—finishes strong, this could be the first unabridged season since 1950 (when teams played 154 games) in which MLB’s second-most-valuable player doesn’t touch 7 WAR. Fittingly, the AL’s MVP contenders are as underwhelming as the AL’s contending teams.
“Underwhelming” doesn’t describe Misiorowski. Of course, the quality that makes the Miz so awe-inspiring—he throws hard enough to remove a mortal’s arm from its socket—is also what makes him so anxiety-inducing. It’s not as if hitters can’t get hurt by running, throwing, or swinging hard—or even by standing somewhere in the vicinity of the on-deck circle, as Crow-Armstrong’s teammate Alex Bregman (whose WAR total since the All-Star break is exceeded only by PCA’s) painfully learned on Sunday. But they aren’t as prone to season-ending disaster as a matter of routine.
We delight in PCA’s uninhibited, prolific play, while we watch the Miz’s impressive but sparing appearances through splayed fingers. As Joe Posnanski pointed out in July, pitching might be the only assignment in sports where “simply doing your job is so scary and treacherous.” Not because an opposing player might flatten you, or because you might, say, stumble and get sliced by a skate blade, but because the fundamental motion endemic to your duty is hazardous to your health. Which helps explain why teams have sought to limit how often pitchers perform that motion, for all the good it’s done them. As it turns out, making that motion more dangerous but doing it less doesn’t make UCLs safer.
Misiorowski has survived the season with only minor, sporadic complaints: a hamstring cramp here, a dead arm there. To forestall more serious trouble, and to preserve their most prized pitcher for the postseason, the Brewers have handled him carefully. Since the All-Star Game (which he missed), he’s tied for 72nd in innings pitched, with two pitchers (Jack Perkins and Zebby Matthews) who have matching 4.94 ERAs over that span. But in October, when off days allow for compression of a pitching staff, an unrestrained Miz may emerge to shoulder more of Milwaukee’s workload and make overmatched opponents and concerned spectators alike quake like Ralph Wiggum. Over a season, or even a series, a position player such as PCA may amass more value. But in any given game, an ace can still slay.

item.content:encoded:
These are the last MLB.com Power Rankings of the 2026 regular season. In exactly one week, 18 of these teams will go home, and 12 will be left. We have made it all the way through. Since these will be the final rankings, let’s take a look at each team, even the ones who did not make the playoffs, and find something positive its fanbase can feel about the 2026 season … now that it’s almost in the rearview mirror.
These rankings, as always, are compiled from MLB.com contributors whose names you can find at the bottom of this (and every) piece, but the words are mine. If you dislike the rankings, yell at all of us. But if you dislike the words, feel free to yell at me.
Also, as we close the season, we note for each team the highest they were ranked in our Power Rankings all season -- when they hit the peak.
1. Brewers (previously: 1)
Season High Water Mark: 1, this week
It’s the best season in Brewers history. It sure looks like they’re going to win 100 games for the first time ever. They’ve got a Cy Young frontrunner in Jacob Misiorowski, they’ve got all the momentum, and they’ve got a team that wins by doing all the little things right. Last year was a huge postseason bummer. Now is the time to right that wrong.
2. Dodgers (previously: 2)
Season High Water Mark: 1, Aug. 17
The Dodgers have had a lot of drama this year, much of it revolving around a hugely disappointing first season at Chavez Ravine for Kyle Tucker and injury concerns for Shohei Ohtani. And yet here they are, one of the best teams in baseball, as always, and the team everyone knows is looming in October.
3. Rays (previously: 4)
Season High Water Mark: 2, May 25
Don’t forget, almost no one picked the Rays to win the tough AL East this year. But it looks like it’s going to be theirs, with a deep, versatile roster led by Junior Caminero, who looks like he’s going to be a signature star in this league for the next decade-plus.
4. Braves (previously: 3)
Season High Water Mark: 1, June 15
Every year since their World Series title in 2021 has felt a little bit like a disappointment in its own way, even the 104-win season in '23. But this one sure hasn’t, with the Braves overcoming a '25 losing season by winning the division again. And check out Ronald Acuña Jr., who looks like a superstar again.
5. Yankees (previously: 5)
Season High Water Mark: 2, May 4
For a long time, it was assumed that if Aaron Judge was hurt for an extended period of time, the Yankees were cooked. But thanks to a fantastic pitching staff -- including Cy Young frontrunner Cam Schlittler -- the Yankees look as strong as ever. But it still may all ride on Judge regardless.
6. Cubs (previously: 6)
Season High Water Mark: 1, May 11
What more can you say about Pete Crow-Armstrong at this point? He’s about to end the Shohei Ohtani MVP reign, and he’s doing so while becoming one of the most popular players in the sport and having one of the best seasons in Cubs history. And it sure feels like October is going to fit him like a glove.
7. Red Sox (previously: 8)
Season High Water Mark: 6, Aug. 5
This season looked absolutely lost in June, and Red Sox fans were tearing their hair out. Then, suddenly, the Sox were playing the best of any team in baseball, and they rode that run all the way to a playoff spot. And it's sure looking like we'll get another installment of The Rivalry in the Wild Card.
8. Padres (previously: 9)
Season High Water Mark: 3, April 20
The Padres have justified all the investments A.J. Preller and company have made in the offseason with this late-season run, but they still have won just one game past the Division Series round this century. The top of the NL is tough this year, but no one’s hotter than the Padres.
9. Phillies (previously: 7)
Season High Water Mark: 5, July 16
It has been a rocky road, with Don Mattingly taking over early in the season, the team righting itself, and then struggling down the stretch. But in this ear, all that matters for the Phillies is the postseason. All of their questions are about to be answered, one way or the other.
10. Guardians (previously: 12)
Season High Water Mark: 5, June 8
The Guardians’ fight back to the top of the AL Central wasn’t as dramatic as last year’s, but if they can end up atop the division when it’s all said and done, it won’t matter. And if they do … they might just get a first-round bye out of it.
11. White Sox (previously: 11)
Season High Water Mark: 6, June 15
If the White Sox aren’t able to get into the playoffs after the fun season they’ve had, it will feel like a heartbreaker, but it probably shouldn’t be. This is a team that has lost 100-plus games for three consecutive seasons! Look at where they are now! The playoffs would be wonderful. But what a major step forward they’ve made. With more to come.
12. Rangers (previously: 16)
Season High Water Mark: 8, April 3
The Rangers have never gotten higher than three games over .500 this year … but that has not kept them out of the middle of the AL West, and even atop the division. They’ve only made the playoffs once in the last decade -- the year they won the World Series. That may well change this season.
13. Diamondbacks (previously: 10)
Season High Water Mark: 9, Aug. 17
The Padres’ torrid run down the stretch may end up keeping Arizona out of the playoffs, though the season’s final series between the two teams could have something to say about that. But a year of uncertainty ended up being a positive one, despite some off-field drama … and there’s still time left in this one.
14. Astros (previously: 13)
Season High Water Mark: 7, April 6
Yordan Alvarez had a fully healthy season and responded with an all-timer of an offensive performance. The only question now is whether they can catch the intrastate-rival Rangers for the AL West crown -- and it looks like they're going to have to, if they want to make the playoffs at all.
15. Blue Jays (previously: 14)
Season High Water Mark: 2, March 23
It looked for a while like the Jays, after the brutal way they lost the World Series last year, would make up for a disappointing season by sneaking into the final Wild Card spot. How fans feel about this season may depend on whether or not they can crawl their way back in. It’s going to be an uphill climb.
16. Pirates (previously: 15)
Season High Water Mark: 5, April 20
Pirates fans had big hopes for this year, and while they weren’t the playoff team that some had expected, they nevertheless have won 79 games and could notch their first winning season since 2018. It’s progress.
17. Orioles (previously: 19)
Season High Water Mark: 10, March 23
It may have hurt to do it, but the O’s did maximize their return for Adley Rutschman with even more young players to add to the ones they already have. It’s understandable if O’s fans are skeptical, but you can’t argue that Pete Alonso was a great investment, and really a North Star for the whole franchise at this point.
18. Marlins (previously: 18)
Season High Water Mark: 8, July 16
Take away that 12-game losing streak, and the Marlins are a playoff team this year. You obviously can’t do that, but the different way the Marlins have been doing things started to pay off this year. And they may well have a star in Otto Lopez.
19. Tigers (previously: 21)
Season High Water Mark: 8, April 27
This turned out to be their first losing season since 2023, which is frustrating because hopes were so high heading into the year, but there is still a ton of young talent here, led by Riley Greene, who is quietly putting together a stellar start to his career. And with the Tarik Skubal trade, there’s even more young talent on the way.
20. Cardinals (previously: 17)
Season High Water Mark: 8, May 18
The bullpen fell apart down the stretch, making the record look worse than the season felt, but the Cardinals made many steps forward this year, particularly with the lineup: Jordan Walker, JJ Wetherholt, Joshua Báez, Alec Burleson and Leo Bernal all look like lineup mainstays … with even more talent coming down the pipe.
21. Nationals (previously: 24)
Season High Water Mark: 12, June 22
James Wood is a star, but he was hardly the only National to emerge in 2026, with CJ Abrams and the recently extended Cade Cavalli setting themselves up as players the Nationals can build around. The offense was terrific this year: That’s the first time you’ve been able to say that in a long time.
22. Mariners (previously: 20)
Season High Water Mark: 3, March 23
So, yeah, it was a bit of a disaster season for the Mariners, in just about every possible way. But this was not a now-or-never season for the M’s: They have a very exciting rotation for 2027, and note that Cal Raleigh started to warm up as the season came to a close as well.
23. Mets (previously: 23)
Season High Water Mark: 5, March 23
That most of the offseason moves blew up in their faces is the reason they’re not in the playoffs, but they certainly played well enough in the second half to look like a playoff team, thanks largely to rookies Carson Benge, A.J. Ewing and Nolan McLean. The Mets will look different next year, but that’s a good thing.
24. Twins (previously: 22)
Season High Water Mark: 15, Aug. 5
The next generation of Twins stars has arrived: Kaelen Culpepper, Walker Jenkins and Emmanuel Rodriguez all made their debut this year (and still have Rookie of the Year eligibility for next season). This was a transition year for the Twins. There’s plenty of reason to think they can turn the corner in 2027.
25. Reds (previously: 25)
Season High Water Mark: 6, April 27
This was the superstar step forward the Reds have been waiting for from Elly De La Cruz. They no longer have to wonder if he’s ever going to make the leap: He now has. And remember, he is still only 24 years old.
26. Royals (previously: 26)
Season High Water Mark: 14, May 11
Not much went the way it was supposed to this year, but there’s still a lot of young talent here. And there is Bobby Witt Jr., who, even in a down power year (for him), leads the American League in WAR, per FanGraphs.
27. Giants (previously: 27)
Season High Water Mark: 18, March 23
The terrible start, and the occasional discord and chaos, made this season feel like it was over with before it even began. But don’t overlook the fact that Rafael Devers, for most of this season, looked like the superstar the Giants traded for.
28. Angels (previously: 29)
Season High Water Mark: 19, April 20
A potential sale of the team is something that fans have wondered could change the trajectory of this franchise, and they’re going to get the opportunity to find out. There’s some young talent starting to percolate here, perhaps most notably Walbert Ureña, a 22-year-old who looks like he might already be an ace.
29. A’s (previously: 28)
Season High Water Mark: 10, May 11
The onslaught of injuries to their position players made people forget how good this lineup was at some point, and how late in the year they were in contention. As they move closer to their move to Las Vegas, there’s still plenty to build on here … and plenty of reason to have optimism for the future.
30. Rockies (previously: 30)
Season High Water Mark: 27, May 4
It does not look like the Rockies are going to avoid 100 losses this year, alas, marking four straight years with 100-plus losses. But they’ll still be double-digit games better than they were last year, and they’ll do so with a front office that seems, at last, to have a clear plan moving forward.
Voters: Jason Catania, Dan Cichalski, Theo DeRosa, Rick Gold Jr., Jared Greenspan, Will Leitch, Brent Maguire, Travis Miller, Brian Murphy, Arturo Pardavila, Shanthi Sepe-Chepuru, Andrew Simon, David Venn, Andy Werle.

item.content:encoded:
A rainy afternoon in Pittsburgh sent the first baseman to the cages early, and the work showed up in the biggest swing of the day.
They did, and he delivered a two-run homer in the seventh inning that put Kansas City ahead.
The lead did not survive an eighth-inning homer by Pittsburgh, and the Royals lost the road finale 4-3, but the way Pasquantino handled an unusual assignment was the most interesting part of a long afternoon.
Built and Lost
Kansas City scored first when first baseman Salvador Perez singled home shortstop Bobby Witt Jr. in the opening inning.
Center fielder Oneil Cruz tied it with a solo homer in the fourth, and first baseman Spencer Horwitz singled home the go-ahead run off starter Michael Wacha in the sixth.
In the seventh, left fielder John Rave reached on a bunt single and moved up on a groundout, and Pasquantino, hitting for center fielder Tyler Tolbert, drove a two-run homer to right center off reliever Carmen Mlodzinski for a 3-2 lead.
Catcher Rafael Flores Jr. answered with a two-run homer in the eighth, and a ninth-inning double by catcher Luke Maile went to waste when the tying run was stranded at third base.
Ready Before He Was Needed
His explanation afterward said plenty about how he goes about the job.
"I got prepared early because I wasn't sure if we would play a full nine innings because of the rain. So I came inside (to the indoor batting) cages in the third or fourth inning. You never feel totally prepared when you come in and pinch-hit in the middle of the game, but I felt good."
Preparation like that usually comes from habit.
Pinch-hitting asks a player to deliver one good at-bat with no rhythm behind it, which makes the preparation part of the job, and Pasquantino treated it that way in a game with nothing on the line.
Wacha did his part too, throwing 113 pitches to protect a tired bullpen because he sensed the relievers needed the rest.
Home for the Final Six
The road schedule is finished, and it ends with Kansas City at 28-53 away from home after a 2-7 trip.
The season closes with six games at Kauffman Stadium, three against the White Sox starting Tuesday and three against the Guardians over the weekend, two clubs separated by one game in the AL Central race.
If the rest of the roster prepares the way Pasquantino did on Sunday, the White Sox and Guardians will have to earn every win they get in Kansas City.

The playoffs technically don't start for another week or so, but good luck telling that to teams for which every game already feels like October. With the standings in both the NL and AL as jumbled as they've been in recent memory, the stakes are already as high as can be — and whoever gets hot now could well ride that wave all the way to a World Series.
"Hot" could definitely describe both the San Diego Padres and Cleveland Guardians of late. The former has decided to just never lose again, not only grabbing hold of a Wild Card spot but now pushing for home-field in the first round if things break right. The latter, meanwhile, has once again snatched the AL Central while no one was looking. And they're not the only ones making serious moves in our latest MLB power rankings.
But who are we buying as serious title contenders, and who still has work to do? Read on to find out.
30. Colorado Rockies
The Rockies have admittedly let go of the rope of late, well on their way to yet another 100-loss season. There are at least some promising young hitters in this organization, which represents something to build upon moving forward. Of course, the pitching staff remains a mess, and no one's been able to crack that nut yet in Colorado.
–Chris Landers, FanSided.com editor
29. Los Angeles Angels
In Reid Detmers, Walbert Urena and Ryan Johnson, the Angels have at least some sort of foundation upon which to build for the future. Well, OK, maybe not Detmers, who will almost certainly be dealt this offseason. But still, L.A.’s pitching staff has been a real bright spot of late. The offense … well, that’s another question. Things are going to get worse before they get better under John Mozeliak. At least Arte Moreno is no longer around to meddle in it.
–CL
28. Athletics
The A’s are playing out the string of a lost season, although the contributions they’ve gotten from young bats like Henry Bolte, Max Muncy (not that one), Lawrence Butler and Zack Gelof down the stretch have been notable. None of that will matter, though, until the team fixes its pitching staff. We know we sound like a broken record, but it really is that simple, and no potential answers have emerged in the second half.
–CL
27. San Francisco Giants
Rafael Devers' injury, which figures to cost him at least some of next season as well as the end of this one, is a fitting if unfortunate end to what's been a miserable season by the Bay. Devers had been one of the few bright spots on this Giants team down the stretch alongside Bryce Eldridge; now, it's unclear how San Francisco will rebuilt its offense for 2027 in addition to finding reinforcements for a pitching staff that simply hasn't been good enough.
–CL
26. Kansas City Royals
The Kansas City Royals have been eliminated for quite some time now. If there is one clear goal for Kansas City this winter, it's to build a roster around Bobby Witt Jr. that is capable of making a postseason run. That is every team's goal, but the Royals are so far away from contention despite featuring such a prolific player, Witt Jr.'s career is closer to becoming Mike Trout's than Derek Jeter's.
-Mark Powell, FanSided.com MLB director
25. Minnesota Twins
At one point not all that long ago, the Twins had a realistic chance to make the playoffs as the third AL Wild Card spot. Then, the bottom fell out. Byron Buxton underwent successful hip surgery just last week that will keep him out until spring training, whenever that may be. The Twins once again experienced the roster flaw of building around an injured star.
-MP
24. New York Mets
This week couldn’t have been more awkward for the New York Mets when Pete Alonso hit his 300th home run in his return to Citi Field, much to the delight of many Mets fans in attendance, but once Alonso left town, the Mets began to play better, winning two games in a row against the Phillies. Those wins, headlined by more quality play from youngsters like Carson Benge, Zac Thornton and Christian Scott, show why Mets fans should be somewhat enthusiastic for what’s to come.
–Zach Rotman, FanSided.com staff writer
23. Cincinnati Reds
In the American League, the Reds likely wouldn't be the worst team in their division. But the NL Central has been a gauntlet all year long, and the Reds couldn't keep up. Despite breakthrough seasons from Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart, Cincinnati still has a long way to go on the starting pitching front. Can they rely on Hunter Greene and Chase Burns moving forward?
-MP
22. Seattle Mariners
Going 3-3 against the Angels and Rockies this week just about sums up this season in Seattle. The good news is that youngsters like Michael Arroyo and Lazaro Montes have helped to key an offensive turnaround. The bad news is that the starting rotation hasn’t held up its end of the bargain of late, and there are still tons of long-term questions about this lineup — especially with Randy Arozarena set to hit free agency. Jerry DiPoto will need to find some answers this offseason after a year in which just about everything went wrong.
–CL
21. Washington Nationals
The Washington Nationals deserved a better fate in 2026. Even with their offense falling off a bit of late, they’re still third in the majors in runs scored. The dynamic duo of CJ Abrams and James Wood is as good as any in the National League. Recently extended Cade Cavalli is a budding ace. Andrew Alvarez has thrown the ball incredibly well and looks like a future rotation stalwart. If it weren’t for a historically bad bullpen, we’d be talking about this team in Wild Card contention.
–ZR
20. Detroit Tigers
The Tigers have the best run differential in the AL Central and a pythagorean record of an AL playoff team. None of it matters. Scott Harris and the Tigers front office gave up on their team's postseason hopes at the trade deadline. Then, they proceeded to get fans' hopes up with a late August run, only to play like the team Harris assumed they'd become when it mattered most. The Tigers have some work to do, though the emergence of young stars in the lineup like Hao-Yu Lee and Kevin McGonigle, paired with Riley Greene's consistent play, give them some building blocks.
-MP
19. St. Louis Cardinals
The Cardinals are ahead of schedule, but not a postseason team. Make no mistake about it, St. Louis came crashing back down to earth in September, and has been eliminated from playoff contention. There are questions about the long-term future of Masyn Winn, especially with JJ Wetherholt as the de-facto shortstop of the future. But these are all good problems to have. Now, if only Bloom could find an ace burried in that farm system of his.
-MP
18. Baltimore Orioles
A series against league-best Milwaukee came at the worst possible time for the O’s, which now find themselves needing to hit an inside straight to snatch the final Wild Card spot. Pete Alonso’s heroics at Citi Field aside, Baltimore’s bats simply have not been good enough. Heck, no part of this team has; they’re hovering around .500 for a reason, after all, and there’s no reason to think they have the consistency required to get hot over the final week and overtake the White Sox, Blue Jays and Astros.
–CL
17. Miami Marlins
The Miami Marlins tried to do what they could to stick around in the NL postseason hunt, even using Sandy Alcantara on one day of rest in a save opportunity, but they were eliminated following Friday’s loss in San Diego. As disappointing as that is, the Marlins could finish above .500 for just the third time since 2009. That’s a sign that things are heading in the right direction for Miami.
–ZR
16. Toronto Blue Jays
The Jays have lost three of four series now, and news that Dylan Cease will have his next start bumped due to shoulder fatigue makes it even less likely that Toronto can sneak its way into the playoffs. With Trey Yesavage and Shane Bieber already on the IL, the rotation has begun leaking oil, and that’s not something this power-starved lineup is equipped to handle. The Jays still have a path to the final Wild Card spot, but it’s becoming an increasingly tenuous one, and it’s hard to see them making much noise even if they did get in.
–CL
15. Houston Astros
Getting swept at home by the Braves this weekend might well wind up costing the Astros a playoff spot. The closing schedule isn’t too tough, with trips to Seattle and Sacramento on tap. Still, if Houston doesn’t figure out where its high-powered offense went before it’s too late — and if Joe Espada can’t stop his bullpen from blowing late leads — Yordan Alvarez’s MVP season may well be for nought. As it stands, this looks like a team with fatal flaws that will spoil what could have been a deep run in a wide-open AL.
–CL
14. Chicago White Sox
Reality hit the White Sox real quick. Chicago has lingered around .500 for longer than they'd care to admit, and it was only a matter of time before the rest of the Central caught up to them. Munetaka Murakami has been dreadful since the trade deadline, and thus any contract extension talks have been put on hold. If the White Sox can hold on to a playoff spot, they'll be one of the best stories in October. If not, this season could all be for naught.
-MP
13. Texas Rangers
All of a sudden, the Rangers find themselves back in control of the AL West and home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs. Of course, that says more about the West than it does about Texas; this is still a .500 team, one without a ton of depth on either side of the ball. The interesting thing, though, is that this lineup has finally started to show signs of life of late. Take care of business against the Twins and Mets this week, and no one’s going to want to face a team with Jacob deGrom and Nathan Eovaldi in the rotation plus an offense featuring Corey Seager, Wyatt Langford and Josh Jung.
-CL
12. Pittsburgh Pirates
The narrative Pirates fans are spinning these days is the same web every National League non-playoff team will get caught in this week; if only we played in the American League! Yes, the disparity between leagues is easy to blame for the Pirates shortcomings, but the front office also fell short in acquiring bullpen arms last winter, which could've kept Pittsburgh from blowing an extraordinary number of leads in the season's first half. That'll haunt these Pirates forever.
-MP
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
It's not Arizona's fault that their primary competition for a Wild Card spot, San Diego, has become one of the hottest teams in baseball over the last few weeks. Either way, though, Arizona has simply run out of bullets, especially in a rotation that hasn't gotten the boost from Corbin Burnes' return that they were hoping for. Eduardo Rodriguez has turned back into a pumpkin, and there's just not enough depth to keep pace with what's become a beast of an NL playoff chase.
–CL
10. Cleveland Guardians
Here we go again with the Guardians. Cleveland is a legitimate threat in a weak American League. Much like last season, the Guards are taking advantage of a fellow contender floundering down the stretch. This is when Cleveland plays its best baseball, so it should be no surprise they've won five straight games heading into Monday's potential postseason preview against the Red Sox.
-MP
9. Boston Red Sox
Dropping consecutive series to the Rangers and Rays won’t do much to Boston’s postseason outlook — they’ve been more or less locked into a Wild Card series in the Bronx for a while now — but it still doesn’t inspire confidence in this team’s ability to make a run come October. This offense is once again mired in a power outage, and while getting Willson Contreras and others back from the IL figures to help, who knows when that might actually be. And there’s still just a real dearth of power here that even this pitching staff might not be able to make up for.
–CL
8. Philadelphia Phillies
I don’t know what to think of the Philadelphia Phillies. On one hand, a rotation led by Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sanchez, a healthy Jesus Luzardo, a rejuvenated Aaron Nola and a much-improved Andrew Painter should will them to wins. On the other hand, Luzardo is not healthy, the lineup is top-heavy and the bullpen, outside of Jhoan Duran, is an utter disaster. The Phillies are almost certainly going to make the playoffs, but their losses in New York this week ruined any last hope they had at a division title. And with how they’re playing right now, I don’t know if I’d pick them to get beyond the Wild Card Round.
–ZR
7. Chicago Cubs
The Cubs playoff parade was put on hold Sunday as Alex Bregman was struck in the face by a foul ball. Bregman was taken to the local hospital, and it's unclear how much time he will miss as of this writing. Chicago's postseason hopes may hang in the balance, as their one clear advantage over every other NL team is their lineup. The Cubs have scored the most runs in baseball this year.
-MP
6. San Diego Padres
Yes, the schedule has helped, particularly series against Miami, Colorado, Washington, San Francisco and Cincinnati. But no matter who they've played, the Padres look like a different team from the one we saw for much of the year, with their big bats finally mashing and their rotation coming into focus with Nick Pivetta now back in the fold. San Diego is now dead even with Chicago and Philly in the Wild Card race, and no one will want to face this lineup and this bullpen in a short series.
–CL
5. New York Yankees
Just when it seemed like New York was getting ready to make a move, with Aaron Judge finally back in the lineup after months on the shelf, the reigning AL MVP landed right back on the IL — this time with a calf strain that could well jeopardize his entire postseason. It’s been that sort of year for the Yankees, which have the pitching to keep believing in them as contenders but just haven’t been able to put it all together enough to take command of their own playoff destiny. And with a Judge-less offense and a penchant for mistake-filled baseball, winning three series in a row feels like a tough ask even in this AL.
–CL
4. Atlanta Braves
The Atlanta Braves punched their ticket to the playoffs this week, and thanks to the Phillies’ struggles, they’re on the cusp of winning the NL East — ensuring a top-three seed in the National League. Tyler Mahle pitched another gem, and Ronald Acuña Jr. is hitting his stride at the perfect time. There’re still some concerns with the team, like the No. 3 spot in their rotation and struggling stars like Austin Riley and Ozzie Albies, but getting to the playoffs is a big deal, and the Braves can take pride in checking that box.
–ZR
3. Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays may well have sewn up the AL East this week, taking two of three from the Red Sox over the weekend to stretch their lead over the Yankees ahead of an all-important four-game set in the Bronx beginning on Tuesday. Even if New York were to sweep all four, though, Tampa would still have the inside track to the division and the No. 1 overall seed. This pitching staff continues to thrive beyond all expectation even with some recent injuries, and the hitting has done just enough. Whether that recipe will withstand the postseason is the only question now.
–CL
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Don't look now, but L.A.'s lineup has begun to stir, with Kyle Tucker looking like the player the Dodgers thought they were paying for this offseason. They also got Edwin Diaz back this week, and he's suddenly looking like the star closer of old — potentially answering this team's biggest question entering October. We know the rotation will be there; if they have Tucker at the height of his powers and a one-two punch in Diaz and Tanner Scott at the end of games, the three-peat march might be back on.
–CL
1. Milwaukee Brewers
The Brewers set a franchise record with 98 wins on Sunday. They still have a full week to go to add to that mark, and appear likely to reach the 100-win plateau. That's a great accomplishment, but it won't mean squat if Milwaukee falls to the Los Angeles Dodgers — or any other NL team for that matter — on their way to that elusive NL pennant. The Brewers are the favorites, but the Dodgers are lingering right behind them.
-MP

item.content:encoded:
Bobby Witt Jr. is having a down year. He’s running his worst batting line in three seasons. He’s in danger of missing the 20-homer threshold for the first time in his career. A lower back injury in July will also limit him to a career low in games played. Put it together, and Witt is on pace to put up his the lowest WAR total since his 5.9-win 2023 campaign. Oh, and he also grabbed hold of the American League lead in WAR back in July and still hasn’t relinquished it. A down year by Bobby Witt Jr.’s standards is still good enough to make him a deserving MVP.
I don’t know if Witt is going to win his first MVP this year. Ours is the only flavor of WAR in which he leads the AL, and he leads by just a quarter of a win. He ranks third by Baseball Reference’s rWAR and is eighth by Baseball Prospectus’ WARP. Yordan Alvarez leads all of baseball in WARP because he’s hitting like, well, Yordan Alvarez and staying healthy like, well, someone other than Yordan Alvarez. Cam Schlittler leads the AL in Baseball Reference WAR, and he’s been so dominant that he deserves consideration for the Cy Young-MVP combo — if only he’d pitched just 23 fewer innings last year, he could’ve gone for the trifecta with Rookie of the Year. Kevin McGonigle has played like an MVP from the moment he arrived in Detroit, and Junior Caminero has surpassed 40 home runs for the second season in a row as a 23-year-old. All of these guys have a case, and they aren’t the only ones who merit inclusion in the discussion:
| Name | fWAR Rk | fWAR | rWAR Rk | rWAR | WARP Rk | WARP | Avg Rk | Avg WAR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bobby Witt Jr. | 1 | 6.6 | 3 | 6.5 | 8 | 5 | 4 | 6.0 |
| Yordan Alvarez | 2 | 6.4 | 4 | 6.4 | 1 | 7.3 | 2 | 6.7 |
| Cam Schlittler | 3 | 6.1 | 1 | 7 | 3 | 5.8 | 2 | 6.3 |
| Dylan Cease | 4 | 5.5 | 8 | 5.7 | 12 | 4.6 | 8 | 5.3 |
| Miguel Vargas | 5 | 5.2 | 10 | 5.3 | 2 | 5.9 | 6 | 5.5 |
| Junior Caminero | 6 | 5.2 | 7 | 5.7 | 5 | 5.3 | 6 | 5.4 |
| Kevin McGonigle | 7 | 5.1 | 2 | 6.7 | 4 | 5.3 | 4 | 5.7 |
| Randy Arozarena | 8 | 5.1 | 11 | 5.3 | 16 | 4 | 12 | 4.8 |
| Dillon Dingler | 9 | 4.6 | 25 | 4 | 23 | 3.3 | 19 | 4.0 |
| Drew Rasmussen | 10 | 4.6 | 21 | 4.2 | 13 | 4.4 | 15 | 4.4 |
| Reid Detmers | 11 | 4.6 | 35 | 3.7 | 11 | 4.7 | 19 | 4.3 |
| Parker Messick | 13 | 4.6 | 6 | 5.8 | 9 | 4.8 | 9 | 5.1 |
| Pete Alonso | 14 | 4.2 | 18 | 4.3 | 6 | 5.3 | 13 | 4.6 |
| Ceddanne Rafaela | 21 | 3.9 | 9 | 5.4 | 94 | 1.7 | 41 | 3.7 |
| Gavin Williams | 27 | 3.7 | 46 | 3.1 | 7 | 5.2 | 27 | 4.0 |
| Wilyer Abreu | 32 | 3.4 | 5 | 5.8 | 20 | 3.6 | 19 | 4.3 |
| Mike Trout | 40 | 3.2 | 28 | 3.9 | 10 | 4.8 | 26 | 4.0 |
Pete Crow-Armstrong, Jacob Misiorowski, Schlittler, McGonigle and JJ Wetherholt have made the AL MVP the only major award that’s really in question). If you want to read a particularly good example, you should check out the one Mario Delgado Genzor wrote for Baseball Prospectus on Friday. I want to focus on something slightly different — namely, how good Witt has already been in years when he missed out on an MVP and how unusual it would be for him to win it this year.
(A quick note before we get into it: We’re about to spend a lot of time talking about WAR. I know I mentioned rWAR and WARP earlier. They’re an important piece of the puzzle, especially due to the outsized effect rWAR in particular has on the MVP conversation, but from here on out, we’re sticking with good old FanGraphs WAR.)
This is Witt’s fifth major league season, and you could argue that it’s his fourth consecutive MVP-caliber campaign. Mind you, that argument would focus only on 2022, in which he put up 5.9 WAR, good for 10th in the majors. There’s no argument to be had about the 2024 and 2025 seasons. That said, along with Shohei Ohtani’s combined 9.2-WAR 2022 sesaon, they are the two most valuable seasons this decade for which a position player did not win an MVP. In 2024, Witt ran a 169 wRC+, stole 31 bases, and put up a Fielding Run Value of 11, fourth among all shortstops. That was good for 10.5 WAR, and it took the best season of Aaron Judge’s career – 58 home runs, a 19% walk rate, and a .322 batting average – to beat him. In 2025, Witt put up 8.0 WAR with a 130 wRC+, 38 steals, and 20 FRV, the best mark among all shortstops. Again, he was bested by a 10-win season from Judge and Cal Raleigh’s 60-homer campaign. Witt has never received a first place MVP vote.
Crow-Armstrong, who has the National League MVP all but locked down, gives us a great example of what it normally takes to win an MVP award. He may even finish with 10.5 WAR through his excellence in all three phases of the game, just like Witt did in 2024. Players like Judge, Ohtani, and Mike Trout, whose base level of talent is so high that a healthy campaign is almost sure to keep them a step above the rest of the league, don’t come around all that often. Even when they do come around, they still need to be playing at something close to their peak, and peaks don’t last that long. Until Ohtani, the only player to win more than three MVPs was Barry Bonds, whose regimen for raising and widening his peak has been well documented. Sometimes that’s because of voter fatigue, but often it’s because somebody else popped up with an amazing, undeniable season like PCA’s. Most of the time, the MVP is an already great player for whom everything goes perfectly. They stay healthy and they play not just their best, but over their heads. Think of Ronald Acuña Jr. winning the NL MVP in 2023 with 9.1 WAR, 4.1 more than his next-best total, or Mookie Betts winning the AL MVP in 2018 with 10.2 WAR, 2.8 more than his next-best total.
Generally speaking, since the voting started getting more rigorous in the last couple decades, those are the two categories of players who win MVPs. We see all-time greats who perform like only they are capable of performing, and we see excellent players who put it all together in a blaze of glory. Witt’s 2024 season probably falls into that second category. He wasn’t quite at his defensive or baserunning peak, but he put up his best season at the plate by nearly 40 points of wRC+ and DRC+, and he ended up with an all-timer of a season. His 10.5 WAR tied for the 36th-best position player campaign of all time. His company? Willie Mays and Babe Ruth twice apiece, Barry Bonds, and Rogers Hornsby. Unfortunately, he ran into one of those special players from the first category, in the form of Judge. If Witt had put up those 2024 numbers this year, he’d be en route to a unanimous MVP just like PCA.
But I said “in theory” earlier, and I said it because Witt isn’t done yet. He’s still just 26, and if not for those weeks he missed with back tightness, or a wOBA that’s more than 30 points below his xwOBA, he’d now be wrapping up his third straight seven-plus-win season. He’s elite in every facet of the game and he doesn’t look like he’s in danger of slowing down any time soon. It wouldn’t be much of a shock to see him rediscover his nine- or 10-win form. In other words, there’s at least a chance Witt belongs to that first category of player and not the second.
Earlier I mentioned Acuña and Betts claiming MVPs by putting up the best years of their careers by a long shot. That’s pretty standard. Especially in recent years, it’s awfully rare for a player to take home an MVP award in something other than the best season of their career, unless they also won the MVP in the best year of their career. Leaving those multi-time MVPs out (and excluding 2020 for obvious reasons), here’s the whole list of players who won an MVP in a year that wasn’t their best by fWAR since 2011: Giancarlo Stanton and Paul Goldschmidt.
Goldschmidt put up 6.8 WAR in his 2022 NL MVP season and 7.2 in 2015. In that sense, Goldschmidt fit a third archetype: the established star who doesn’t put up their biggest WAR total, and instead wins MVP as something of a career achievement award. Stanton put up 6.5 WAR in 2017, not quite the 6.8-win campaign he put up in 2014, but he was facing a weaker field, he was more established as a star, and he had the cachet of a 59-homer season. We’re talking about gaps of less than half a win. We had some multi-time winners, but Acuña, Betts, Cody Bellinger, Christian Yelich, Jose Altuve, Kris Bryant, Josh Donaldson, Andrew McCutchen, and Buster Posey all won MVP in the best seasons of their career by fWAR.
Let’s say that Witt does win the MVP this year. For the sake of round numbers, let’s say he closes strong and finishes with 7.0 WAR. That would be just the third-best season of his career, and a full 3.5 WAR below his career-high. Baseball Reference lists MVP winners going back to 1911, and in that time, Witt would become just the ninth position player to win MVP in a season that trailed their best year by such a wide margin. The list of players to do it before him is full of three-time MVPs like Joe DiMaggio, Mickey Mantle, and Mike Schmidt. Not only that, but you’ll note that if Witt does make this list, the only higher number in either column will belong to Mantle:
| Player | MVP Year | MVP WAR | Best Year | Best WAR | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frankie Frisch | 1931 | 4.1 | 1927 | 9.7 | 5.6 |
| Mickey Mantle | 1962 | 6.0 | 1956 | 11.5 | 5.5 |
| Willie Stargell | 1979 | 2.7 | 1971 | 8.2 | 5.4 |
| Joe DiMaggio | 1947 | 4.8 | 1941 | 9.7 | 4.9 |
| Freddie Freeman | 2020* | 3.0 | 2023 | 7.7 | 4.7 |
| Robin Yount | 1989 | 5.3 | 1982 | 9.8 | 4.5 |
| Andre Dawson | 1987 | 3.5 | 1982 | 7.3 | 3.8 |
| Mike Schmidt | 1986 | 5.8 | 1974 | 9.4 | 3.6 |
| Roger Peckinpaugh | 1925 | 2.4 | 1919 | 5.9 | 3.5 |
The last person to do so was Robin Yount, who won the AL MVP with 9.8 WAR in 1982, and then again with 5.3 WAR in 1989, long before anybody knew that Total Zone considered him the 11th-worst defender in the majors. This hasn’t happened in nearly 30 years, and Witt is in a very different boat here. He’s not one of the two MVP favorites because his season looks great to the eye but doesn’t fool the advanced metrics. He’s not an aging star who can count on some lifetime-achievement votes. He’s a young gun who’s leading his league in WAR because he excels in every facet of the game.
I realize that this is far from the most meticulous analysis I’ve ever conducted, and that MVP voting is and should be about more than WAR. Still, I hope I’ve put this season in the context it deserves. By our measuring stick, Witt has been the best player in the American League this season. He’s done so despite missing time due to injury. He’s done so despite some bad batted ball luck. And he’s done so despite not even coming close to the highest gear we know he’s got available to him, because that gear is so high that it’s normally reserved for inner-circle Hall of Famers. However the voting goes, Witt’s been in MVP form for three or four years now.
Davy Andrews is a Brooklyn-based musician and a writer at FanGraphs. He can be found on Bluesky @davyandrewsdavy.bsky.social.

NEW YORK (AP) — Cristopher Sánchez earned his major league-leading 18th win Sunday, leading the Philadelphia Phillies to a 7-2 victory over the New York Mets.
The Phillies (86-70), who salvaged a split of the four-game series, entered Sunday in the third National League wild-card spot, one game behind the Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres and four games clear of the Arizona Diamondbacks.
Sánchez surrendered six hits — including Bo Bichette’s sixth-inning homer — and struck out six over 6 1/3 innings as he snapped a tie with the Boston Red Sox’s Sonny Gray for the big league lead in wins.
